traps.title: Integer cache and ==
options: Compile error: cannot compare Integer objects with ==
traps.commonWrongAnswer: true and true, because both pairs hold the same number.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Because `==` compares values for `int`, candidates assume it does the same for `Integer`, and small test values
(1, 42, 100) always seem to 'work'. They don't realise that autoboxing calls `Integer.valueOf()`, which hands out
cached objects only for a fixed range. So `==` on wrappers is really an identity check that only happens to look like
value equality for small numbers.
traps.correct:
`Integer a = 127` compiles to `Integer.valueOf(127)`. `valueOf` returns a shared instance from the internal
`IntegerCache` for values from -128 to 127, so `a` and `b` are the **same object** and `a == b` is `true`. 128 is
outside the cache, so `c` and `d` are two different objects and `c == d` is `false`. On references, `==` always
compares identity, never value.

The upper bound can be raised with `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax`, one more reason never to depend on it. `Byte`, `Short`,
`Long` (-128..127) and `Character` (0..127) cache too; `Float`/`Double` don't. A related trap:
`Long.valueOf(127L).equals(127)` is `false`, because the argument boxes to an `Integer`, which is a different type.
traps.fix:
```java
a.equals(b);                    // value comparison
Objects.equals(c, d);           // null-safe value comparison
c.intValue() == d.intValue();   // explicit unboxing (NPE if either is null)
```
traps.interviewTip: Mention how this bites in production: IDs or counts compared with == pass tests with small values and break once real data goes past 127.

traps.title: String pool, intern() and ==
traps.commonWrongAnswer: false true true: they assume any concatenation that produces "hello" ends up in the pool.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Most people know that `new String()` creates a separate object, but they think every string equal to a literal gets
pooled automatically. Pooling is automatic only for **compile-time constants**. A concatenation involving a non-final
variable is evaluated at runtime (through `invokedynamic` string concatenation) and always produces a new heap object.
traps.correct:
String literals are interned, so `s1` points to the pooled "hello". `new String("hello")` always allocates a new
object, so `s1 == s2` is `false`. `intern()` returns the canonical pooled instance, so `s3` is the same object as `s1`:
`true`. `part + "lo"` is not a constant expression because `part` is an ordinary variable. It is built at runtime into
a new object, so `false`.

If `part` were declared `final String part = "hel";` it would become a compile-time constant. The compiler would then
fold `part + "lo"` into the literal "hello", and `s1 == s4` would be `true`. Since Java 7 the pool lives on the main
heap, not in PermGen. The rule: compare strings with `equals()`, and use `==` only when you really want identity.
traps.fix:
```java
s1.equals(s4);              // true
"hello".equals(input);      // literal first: no NPE when input is null
s1.equalsIgnoreCase(other);
```
traps.interviewTip: Bring up the `final` variable case yourself. Knowing that constant folding changes the answer shows you understand compile time versus runtime, not just the rule.

traps.title: equals() without hashCode() in a HashSet
traps.commonWrongAnswer: 1 true, because equals() says the two people are equal, so the set rejects the duplicate.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates think `HashSet` and `HashMap` decide equality with `equals()` alone. In fact the hash is used first to pick
a bucket, and `equals()` is called only for entries in that same bucket. If `hashCode()` doesn't match, two 'equal'
objects almost always land in different buckets, and `equals()` is never called at all.
traps.correct:
`HashSet` is backed by a `HashMap`. On `add` it computes `hashCode()` to choose a bucket. Only for entries in that
bucket with the same hash does it call `equals()`. `Object.hashCode()` is identity-based, so the two `Person` objects
get different hashes and both are stored. The size is 2 (in practice; only a freak identity-hash collision could
change that). `contains(new Person("Raj"))` computes yet another identity hash, looks in the wrong bucket and returns
`false`.

This breaks the contract in `Object`: equal objects **must** have equal hash codes. The reverse doesn't hold: unequal
objects may share a hash (a collision), and the bucket handles that. Since Java 8 a heavily collided bucket turns into
a balanced tree, which helps performance but changes nothing about correctness. Use the same fields in `equals` and
`hashCode`.
traps.interviewTip: State the contract in both directions (equal means same hash; same hash does not mean equal) and mention that records generate both methods for value types.

traps.title: Mutating a HashMap key after put()
traps.commonWrongAnswer: order-1 for get(k), because it is literally the same object that was put in.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
People picture a HashMap as holding on to the key object and finding it again by identity. They forget that the entry
was filed under the hash computed **at put time**. Changing a field used by `hashCode()` changes where lookups go, but
the entry stays where it was. A lookup with the old value reaches the right bucket but then fails the `equals()` check.
traps.correct:
At `put`, the entry is stored in the bucket for hash(1). After `k.id = 2`, `get(k)` computes hash(2), looks in a
different bucket and finds nothing, so it returns `null`. `get(new Key(1))` reaches the right bucket, but the stored key
now has id 2, so `equals()` fails and that's `null` too. The entry is still there (`size()` is 1 and
`containsValue("order-1")` is `true`), but no key can reach it. That's a silent leak and a source of 'lost' data.

The same applies to `HashSet` elements and to `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` entries whose `compareTo` fields change. Keys should
be immutable: `String`, `Integer`, records with immutable components, or classes whose hash fields are `final`. JPA
entities with generated ids hit this when they are added to a `HashSet` before the id is assigned.
traps.interviewTip: Say 'hash-based collections need keys whose hashCode never changes while they are inside', and connect it to why String is immutable.

traps.title: Removing inside for-each (and the second-to-last quirk)
traps.commonWrongAnswer: It throws ConcurrentModificationException, because you can never remove from a list inside a for-each loop.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
'Removing inside for-each throws CME' is taught as an absolute rule, so people pattern-match on it. The exception
actually comes from the iterator's `next()`, when it notices that `modCount` has changed. If the loop ends before
`next()` is called again, nothing checks, and the bug stays hidden. Silent wrong behaviour is worse than an exception.
traps.correct:
The for-each loop uses an `Iterator`. `hasNext()` only checks `cursor != size`. `next()` checks
`modCount == expectedModCount` and throws CME on a mismatch. When "B" (index 1) is removed, the cursor is already 2
and the size drops to 2. `hasNext()` returns `false`, the loop exits without calling `next()` again, there's no
exception, and `[A, C]` is printed. Removing the **second-to-last** element always behaves like this, and the last
element is never visited, so a check on it would silently be skipped.

Remove "A" instead, and the next `next()` call throws CME. Removing "C" throws too: `hasNext()` sees cursor 3 != size 2,
so the loop calls `next()`, which throws. CME is a best-effort, fail-fast bug detector, not a guarantee, and it happens in a single
thread. It has nothing to do with multithreading.
traps.fix:
```java
list.removeIf(s -> s.equals("B"));                 // simplest and clearest

Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();              // when you need more logic
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next().equals("B")) it.remove();         // iterator's own remove keeps modCount in sync
}

List<String> kept = list.stream().filter(s -> !s.equals("B")).toList(); // build a new list
```
traps.interviewTip: Explain modCount/expectedModCount and say CME is only 'best effort', so a passing test doesn't prove the loop is correct.

traps.title: Arrays.asList vs List.of vs unmodifiable views
traps.commonWrongAnswer: It prints [X, y, z, w], because Arrays.asList returns an ArrayList.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
The returned class really is called `ArrayList`, but it's the private nested class `java.util.Arrays$ArrayList`: a
fixed-size view over the array, not `java.util.ArrayList`. Candidates also treat all the 'read-only' factories as the
same thing, without knowing that `Arrays.asList`, `List.of`, `Collections.unmodifiableList` and `Stream.toList()` each
follow different rules.
traps.correct:
`Arrays.asList` returns a **fixed-size list backed by the array**. `set()` works and writes through to the array (and
changes to the array show up in the list), but `add`/`remove` throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. So the `set`
succeeds and the `add` throws.

`List.of(...)` is fully immutable. `set`, `add` and `remove` all throw, null elements are rejected with
`NullPointerException`, and even `contains(null)` throws NPE. `Collections.unmodifiableList(src)` is a read-only
**view**: you can't change the list through it, but later changes to `src` still show through. `Stream.toList()`
(Java 16) returns an unmodifiable list that does allow nulls. `Collectors.toList()` currently returns a mutable
`ArrayList` but doesn't promise to. Finally, `Arrays.asList(new int[]{1,2,3})` is a `List<int[]>` of size 1.
traps.fix:
```java
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList("x", "y", "z")); // mutable copy
List<String> safe = List.copyOf(input);                             // immutable defensive copy for APIs
List<Integer> ints = Arrays.stream(new int[]{1, 2, 3}).boxed().toList();
```
traps.interviewTip: Contrast unmodifiable views with truly immutable copies (List.copyOf). It shows you think about defensive copying at API boundaries.

traps.title: finally vs return
traps.commonWrongAnswer: 2 2: since finally runs last, they reason that its changes win in both methods.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates know that `finally` always runs after `try`, so they assume it 'has the last word' on the result. They
don't separate two different cases: changing a local variable after the return value has **already been evaluated**,
and executing a new `return` statement that replaces the pending one.
traps.correct:
In `a()`, `return x` evaluates `x` (1) and saves that value before the finally block runs. Assigning `x = 2` changes
the local variable, not the saved return value, so `a()` returns 1. If `x` were a mutable object such as a
`StringBuilder`, changes to the object *would* be visible, because the saved value is the reference.

In `b()`, `return 2` inside finally completes the method abruptly and discards the pending `return 1`, so it returns 2.
A `return` in finally also **swallows exceptions**: `try { throw new RuntimeException(); } finally { return 3; }`
returns 3 and the exception disappears. That's why javac (`-Xlint:finally`) and linters warn about it. A finally
block is skipped only if the JVM halts (`System.exit`, a crash, `kill -9`) or the thread never leaves the try.
traps.interviewTip: Mention that a return in finally silently swallows exceptions. That's the production consequence interviewers want to hear.

traps.title: Overloading with null, widening, boxing, varargs
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Object / Integer: null 'is an Object', and 5 is 'closest to' Integer.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
People treat overload resolution as 'pick the closest-looking type' instead of the actual compile-time algorithm. Two
rules surprise them. With `null`, the **most specific** applicable type wins, and `String` is a subclass of `Object`.
And the compiler tries widening before boxing, and boxing before varargs, so widening the primitive to `long` beats
boxing it to `Integer`.
traps.correct:
Overloads are chosen at compile time in three phases: (1) exact match or primitive widening, with no boxing or
varargs; (2) boxing/unboxing allowed; (3) varargs allowed. For `n(5)`, phase 1 already finds `n(long)` through
int-to-long widening, so boxing to `Integer` is never considered. Remove `n(long)` and you get `Integer`; remove that
too and you get varargs.

For `m(null)`, both `m(Object)` and `m(String)` accept null, and Java picks the most specific one, `String`. Add
`m(Integer)` and the call no longer compiles ("reference to m is ambiguous"), because `String` and `Integer` are
unrelated and neither is more specific. Overriding is different: it is resolved at runtime from the object's actual
class, while overloading uses the declared (static) types of the arguments.
traps.fix:
Avoid overloads that differ only by primitive/boxed or related parameter types. Give them distinct names, or cast to
choose explicitly:

```java
static void logId(long id) { /* ... */ }
static void logIds(int... ids) { /* ... */ }

m((Object) null);   // explicit choice when an overload set is unavoidable
```
traps.interviewTip: Name the three phases (widening, then boxing, then varargs) and contrast compile-time overloading with runtime overriding.

traps.title: Integer overflow and Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)
traps.prompt:
A service routes keys to one of 10 shards:

```java
int shard = Math.abs(key.hashCode()) % 10;
```

Can `shard` ever be negative? What does `System.out.println(Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE));` print?
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Math.abs always returns a non-negative number, so shard is always between 0 and 9.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Developers think of `int` as a mathematical integer. The two's-complement range is asymmetric, -2,147,483,648 to
2,147,483,647, so the absolute value of `Integer.MIN_VALUE` doesn't fit. Java integer arithmetic silently wraps around
instead of throwing, so the bug never shows up in tests that use 'normal' keys.
traps.correct:
`Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` overflows and returns `Integer.MIN_VALUE` itself, which is still negative. If a key's
`hashCode()` is exactly `Integer.MIN_VALUE` (the string "polygenelubricants" is a known example),
`Math.abs(h) % 10` is -8 and you route to a shard that doesn't exist. Java `int`/`long` arithmetic never throws on
overflow: `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1` is `Integer.MIN_VALUE`.

The same family of bugs: binary search's `(low + high) / 2` goes negative for large indices (use
`low + (high - low) / 2` or `(low + high) >>> 1`), and `24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 1000` is computed in `int` (giving
500654080 instead of 86400000000) even when the result is assigned to a `long`.
traps.fix:
```java
int shard = Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), 10);   // always 0..9
int mid   = low + (high - low) / 2;
long micros = 24L * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 1000;        // force long arithmetic from the first operand
int total = Math.addExact(a, b);                  // throws ArithmeticException on overflow
int abs   = Math.absExact(x);                     // Java 15+: throws for Integer.MIN_VALUE
```
traps.interviewTip: Use the shard/bucket example. It shows you have seen the bug in a real system rather than memorised a puzzle.

traps.title: BigDecimal equals vs compareTo, new BigDecimal(0.1)
traps.commonWrongAnswer: true true and 0.1: BigDecimal is 'exact', so 2.0 equals 2.00 and 0.1 stays 0.1.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates know BigDecimal is the right type for money, so they assume it behaves like a mathematical number
everywhere. But `equals()` compares the value **and the scale**. And the `double` constructor faithfully copies the
binary approximation of 0.1, which was already inexact before BigDecimal ever saw it.
traps.correct:
`BigDecimal.equals` takes scale into account: 2.0 (scale 1) and 2.00 (scale 2) are not equal. `compareTo` compares the
numeric value only and returns 0. In practice, a `HashSet<BigDecimal>` keeps both values (size 2) while a `TreeSet`,
which uses compareTo, keeps one. And `assertEquals(new BigDecimal("2.0"), amountFromDb)` fails when the DB column has
scale 2.

`new BigDecimal(0.1)` converts the exact binary value of the double, giving
0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625. `BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)` (which goes through
`Double.toString`) and `new BigDecimal("0.1")` both give 0.1. Also, `divide` without a scale and rounding mode throws
`ArithmeticException` for non-terminating results such as 1/3.
traps.fix:
```java
a.compareTo(b) == 0;                              // value equality
BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("0.10");        // build from String
BigDecimal p2 = BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1);          // if you only have a double
BigDecimal share = total.divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(3), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
BigDecimal stored = amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP); // normalise scale before storing/comparing
```
traps.interviewTip: Say you'd normalise money to a fixed scale (or store minor units such as paise in a long) and compare with compareTo. Fintech interviewers listen for exactly that.

traps.title: Stream laziness, short-circuiting and reuse
options: F1 F2 F3 F4 M2 M4 start 20
start F1 F2 F3 F4 M2 M4 20
traps.commonWrongAnswer: F1 F2 F3 F4 M2 M4 start 20: each operation runs over the whole list as soon as it is declared, like one loop per step.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
People imagine a stream pipeline as a series of loops: filter everything into a new collection, then map everything.
Streams are lazy. Nothing runs until a terminal operation pulls elements, and then each element travels through the
whole chain one at a time. Short-circuiting operations stop pulling as soon as they have an answer.
traps.correct:
Intermediate operations (`filter`, `map`, `peek`, `sorted`, ...) only build a pipeline. Nothing runs until a terminal
operation (`findFirst`, `collect`, `count`, `forEach`), so "start" prints first. Then elements flow one by one: 1 fails
the filter, 2 passes and is mapped to 20, and `findFirst` short-circuits. 3 and 4 are never touched.

Two related traps. A stream can be consumed only once: a second terminal call throws
`IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed`. And since Java 9, `count()` may skip the
pipeline entirely when the size is known in advance, so `List.of("a","b").stream().peek(System.out::println).count()`
prints nothing. Never put side effects you rely on inside `peek` or `map`.
traps.interviewTip: Mention the Java 9 count() shortcut with peek. It shows you know laziness is an optimisation contract, not just 'streams are lazy'.

traps.title: Optional.orElse is eager
traps.prompt:
```java
public User getUser(long id) {
    return cache.find(id)                 // returns Optional<User>
                .orElse(loadFromDb(id));  // loadFromDb queries MySQL
}
```

The user is almost always in the cache. How often is `loadFromDb` called?
options: On every call, even on a cache hit
Only the first time, because Optional memoizes it
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Only on a cache miss, because orElse is the 'fallback'.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
`orElse` reads like an if/else, so people assume the fallback is evaluated only when needed. But it is an ordinary
method call. Java evaluates all arguments **before** calling a method, so `loadFromDb(id)` runs first and its result is
passed in, then quietly thrown away whenever the Optional already has a value.
traps.correct:
`orElse(T other)` takes a value, so the argument expression is evaluated eagerly on every call. The DB query runs on
every cache hit and its result is discarded. That's a hidden performance bug, and a correctness bug if the fallback has
side effects such as inserting a default record. `orElseGet(Supplier<T>)` takes a lambda and calls it only when the
Optional is empty. Use `orElse` only for constants or values you have already computed.

Related Optional traps: `Optional.of(null)` throws `NullPointerException` (use `ofNullable`); `get()` on an empty
Optional throws `NoSuchElementException` (prefer `orElseThrow()`); and Optional is meant as a return type, not for
fields, parameters or collections.
traps.interviewTip: Point out the side-effect angle: an `orElse(createDefaultUser())` that inserts a row on every call is the version that causes real incidents.

traps.title: List.remove(int) vs remove(Object)
traps.commonWrongAnswer: [10, 20, 30]: remove(1) removes the element 1.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates expect autoboxing to turn `1` into an `Integer` and call `remove(Object)`. But `List` has two overloads,
`remove(int index)` and `remove(Object o)`, and overload resolution prefers an exact primitive match over boxing. So
the index version wins and a completely different element disappears, with no error and no warning.
traps.correct:
Overload resolution first tries methods that need no boxing. `remove(int)` matches the `int` literal exactly, so it
removes the element **at index 1** (20) and leaves `[10, 30, 1]`. To remove the value 1, pass an object:
`ids.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))` gives `[10, 20, 30]`.

The trap is nastier than it looks. `Collection` and `Set` have only `remove(Object)`, so the same line removes by value
when the variable is declared as `Collection<Integer>` or `Set<Integer>`, and by index once someone refactors it to
`List<Integer>`. With a `List<Long>` and a `long` argument it removes by value, because `long` can't narrow to `int`.
These differences come from compile-time types, not from the runtime object.
traps.fix:
```java
ids.remove(Integer.valueOf(1));      // remove by value
ids.removeIf(id -> id == 1);         // clearest intent; removes all matches
int removedAt = ids.indexOf(1);      // if you really mean an index, compute it explicitly
```
traps.interviewTip: Mention the Set-to-List refactoring case. It shows you think about how code can silently change meaning, not just about the puzzle.

traps.title: volatile is not atomic (count++)
options: Always 200000, because volatile makes every update visible
Usually less than 200000 and different on each run (occasionally exactly 200000)
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Always 200000, because volatile makes the variable thread-safe.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
`volatile` handles visibility and ordering, and candidates stretch that into 'thread-safe'. But `count++` is three
steps: read, add one, write. volatile does nothing to make those three steps indivisible. Two threads can read the same
value and both write back value + 1, so one increment is lost.
traps.correct:
`volatile` guarantees that every read sees the latest write and that accesses aren't reordered around it (a
happens-before edge). It does **not** give mutual exclusion. `count++` is a read, an add and a write, and if two threads
interleave as read, read, write, write, one increment is lost. On Java 21 this printed values such as 159013 and
152672, and occasionally exactly 200000. That last case is why these bugs survive testing.

Use volatile for a flag (`volatile boolean running`), a value with a single writer, or safe publication of an
immutable object. For read-modify-write use `AtomicInteger` (a CAS loop), `LongAdder` for heavily contended counters,
or a lock. The database version of this bug is the same: read a value into Java, add to it, and write it back.
traps.interviewTip: Separate the three guarantees (atomicity, visibility, ordering) and say that volatile gives only the last two.

traps.title: synchronized on the wrong monitor
options: Always 200000, because the method is synchronized
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Always 200000, because increment() is synchronized.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates see the `synchronized` keyword and stop there, without asking **which** monitor is locked. A synchronized
instance method locks `this`. Two different Counter instances therefore hold two different locks and never block each
other, while the data being protected is a static field that both of them share.
traps.correct:
A synchronized instance method is shorthand for `synchronized (this)`. `c1` and `c2` are different objects, so the two
threads take different monitors and run `count++` on the shared static field at the same time, and increments are
lost (real runs printed 131486 and 184604). Everyone who touches the data must lock the **same** object, and the lock's
scope must match the data's scope. For static data that means `static synchronized` (which locks `Counter.class`) or a
`static final` lock object.

The same family of bugs: `synchronized (new Object())` (a fresh lock on every call, so no exclusion at all); locking a
field that gets reassigned (`Integer lock; lock++` creates a new object); locking a String literal or boxed Integer
that unrelated code may share; and guarding writes while reading without the lock.
traps.interviewTip: Ask out loud: 'Which object is the monitor, and does every access to this data use that same monitor?'

traps.title: Double-checked locking without volatile
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Yes. The second null check inside synchronized prevents two instances, so it's safe.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates only think about the 'two instances' race, and the inner check does prevent that. They miss the visibility
problem. The outer `if` reads `instance` without any lock, so there is no happens-before relationship with the thread
that wrote it. That reader can see the reference before it sees the writes made inside the constructor.
traps.correct:
`instance = new Config(...)` is roughly: allocate memory, run the constructor (write the fields), publish the
reference. The JIT and the CPU may reorder these steps. Even without reordering, a thread that never enters
`synchronized` has no guarantee of seeing the constructor's writes. So thread B can pass the outer `if`, get a non-null
`instance`, and read default values (null or 0) from its fields: a **partially constructed object**.

The fix is to declare the field `volatile`. A volatile write happens-before every later volatile read of it, so the
constructor's writes become visible. Alternatives are the initialization-on-demand holder idiom (the JVM makes class
initialization lazy and thread-safe) and an `enum` singleton. If every field of `Config` is `final`, the Java Memory
Model guarantees other threads see them initialized, but relying on that is subtle. In Spring code, just make it a
singleton bean.
traps.interviewTip: Use the terms 'safe publication' and 'happens-before', and offer the holder idiom as the cleaner option.

traps.title: ConcurrentHashMap check-then-act race
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Always 200000, because ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
'Thread-safe collection' gets heard as 'my code that uses it is thread-safe'. ConcurrentHashMap makes each single call
atomic, but a `get` followed by a `put` is two calls. Another thread can update the value between them, and one update
overwrites the other. That is a check-then-act (read-modify-write) race in your code, not in the map.
traps.correct:
Every individual method of ConcurrentHashMap is atomic, but compound actions built from several calls are not. Two
threads both read 41, both put 42, and one hit is gone. Real runs printed values such as 97642 and 82200 instead of
200000. The same race appears in `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, create())`, which can create two values and
leave one caller holding an object that isn't in the map.

Use the atomic compound methods: `merge`, `compute`, `computeIfAbsent`, `putIfAbsent` and `replace(k, old, new)`. Keep
the functions you pass to `compute`/`computeIfAbsent` short. They run while part of the map is locked, so slow I/O
blocks other writers, and modifying the same map inside them can throw `IllegalStateException: Recursive update`.
ConcurrentHashMap also rejects null keys and values.
traps.fix:
```java
hits.merge("home", 1, Integer::sum);                                   // atomic increment

ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> counters = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
counters.computeIfAbsent("home", k -> new LongAdder()).increment();    // best for hot counters

Lock lock = locks.computeIfAbsent(orderId, k -> new ReentrantLock());  // create-once, cheap factory
```
traps.interviewTip: Say 'each call is atomic, sequences of calls are not', and reach for merge/computeIfAbsent before being prompted.

traps.title: Plain HashMap shared between threads
traps.commonWrongAnswer: With distinct keys the worst case is a slightly stale read; a HashMap can't actually break.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
People picture a HashMap as independent slots, one per key. Internally, all keys share one table array, a size
counter, and bucket lists or trees, and any put can trigger a resize that rebuilds the whole table. Unsynchronized
writers to *any* keys race on that shared structure, not just writers to the same key.
traps.correct:
HashMap's internal state (the `table` array, the bucket chains, `size`, `modCount`) is shared by all keys. Concurrent
puts can overwrite each other's bucket links, or both resize at once, and entries vanish. In a test, 4 threads
inserting 100,000 distinct keys ended with sizes like 63,912 and 78,173. Readers can also get `null` for a key that is
present, because without synchronization there's no visibility guarantee, and a resize may be half done.

In Java 7, a concurrent resize could create a cycle in a bucket's linked list, leaving `get()` spinning at 100% CPU
forever, a classic production incident. Java 8 changed resizing, but concurrent use is still undefined behaviour:
lost data, a wrong `size()`, even exceptions in tree bins. Use `ConcurrentHashMap`, or a cache library such as Caffeine
when you need size limits and expiry. `Collections.synchronizedMap` works, but it has one global lock, and you must
lock it yourself while iterating.
traps.interviewTip: Mention the Java 7 infinite-loop incident, then add that an unbounded map used as a cache is a memory leak anyway: size limits matter as much as thread safety.

traps.title: ThreadLocal leaking across pooled requests
options: Always null, because ThreadLocal values are cleared when the request ends
Always null, because ThreadLocal keys are weak references and get garbage-collected
The tenant of an earlier request that ran on the same pooled thread
traps.commonWrongAnswer: null: the value belonged to the previous request, and a ThreadLocal is cleaned up after each request.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Developers treat a request and a thread as the same thing. With a thread pool, the thread outlives the request and gets
reused, and nothing in Java or Tomcat clears your ThreadLocal for you. Many also half-remember that ThreadLocalMap uses
weak references, and assume that means automatic cleanup.
traps.correct:
A ThreadLocal value lives in the `ThreadLocalMap` of the thread itself. Pooled threads are not destroyed between
requests, so the value set by request 1 is still there when request 2 runs on the same thread. Here, a request without
the header reads another tenant's id: a **data leak across customers**. (In a test, a one-thread pool handed 'alice'
to the next task.)

The map's *keys* are weak references to the ThreadLocal object, but the *values* are strong. While the static
ThreadLocal exists nothing is collected, and on redeploys stale values can pin whole classloaders in memory. Always
`remove()` in a finally block. The same applies to the logging MDC and the security context. Virtual threads (one per
task, never pooled) don't bleed values between tasks, but each thread gets its own copy, so heavy per-thread caches
multiply memory. `ScopedValue` (final in Java 25) is the modern alternative.
traps.interviewTip: Frame it as a security bug (one customer seeing another's data), not just a memory leak. That framing is what makes the answer senior-level.

traps.title: Deadlock from inconsistent lock order
traps.commonWrongAnswer: It's fine: both blocks are synchronized, so the transfers just run one after the other.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates think more locking means more safety. Each lock on its own is fine; the danger is the **order**. Thread 1
holds `a` and waits for `b`, while thread 2 holds `b` and waits for `a`. `synchronized` has no timeout, so both wait
forever, and the code passes every single-threaded test.
traps.correct:
This is a classic deadlock. All four Coffman conditions hold: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and
circular wait (T1 goes a then b, T2 goes b then a). With a short pause between the two locks, both threads hang every
time. `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` reports 2 threads, and a `jstack` thread dump prints "Found one Java-level
deadlock".

The standard fix breaks circular wait by taking locks in a **global order**, for example by account id, whatever the
transfer direction. Alternatives: `ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout)` with back-off and retry, or one coarser lock if
throughput allows. In a real system the money lives in the database, and the same rule applies there: lock rows in a
consistent order (`SELECT ... WHERE id IN (?, ?) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE`) or use one atomic conditional UPDATE, and
handle the database's deadlock errors with a retry.
traps.interviewTip: Name the four Coffman conditions, break circular wait with lock ordering, and then map the same idea to SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in MySQL.

traps.title: parallelStream with shared mutable state
options: Unpredictable: fewer than 100000, null elements inside, or an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Always 100000, just in a random order
Compile error: forEach needs a thread-safe list
traps.commonWrongAnswer: 100000, just in a random order: parallel only changes the order.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
`parallel()` looks like a free speed-up switch, so people assume the program still means the same thing. In fact it
runs the lambda on several ForkJoinPool threads at once, and `ArrayList.add` changes shared state (the size field and
the backing array) with no synchronization at all.
traps.correct:
The pipeline splits the range across common-pool worker threads, and each of them calls `out.add` concurrently.
ArrayList's `size++` and array growth race with each other. Real runs gave 63,641 elements including 5,167 nulls, then
64,777, then an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. The fix is to not mutate shared state from a stream at all: let the
stream build the result with `toList()`/`collect`, which gives each thread its own container and merges them safely.

A second trap: parallel streams run on `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` (about cores - 1 threads), which the whole JVM shares,
including `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync` without an executor. Blocking I/O inside a parallel stream (HTTP or DB calls)
starves everyone else using that pool. Parallel streams only pay off for large, CPU-bound work on sources that split
well.
traps.interviewTip: Say 'parallel streams share the common pool' and that you would never put blocking calls in them. That's the production lesson.

traps.title: CompletableFuture swallows exceptions
options: A stack trace from the worker thread's uncaught-exception handler, then "done"
Only "done": the exception is stored in the future and nobody ever sees it
The exception propagates to the caller and "done" is never printed
The JVM exits with a non-zero code
traps.commonWrongAnswer: A stack trace gets printed, just like an exception in a plain Thread.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
With `new Thread(...)`, an uncaught exception reaches the default uncaught-exception handler, which prints a stack
trace, and candidates expect the same here. But CompletableFuture catches the exception and completes the future
exceptionally. If nobody calls `get`/`join` or attaches a handler, the failure is silently dropped.
traps.correct:
`runAsync`/`supplyAsync` wrap the task, so any exception completes the future exceptionally and stays inside it. The
program prints only `done`: no log line, no stack trace. You see the error only when you observe the future. `get()`
throws a checked `ExecutionException` and `join()` an unchecked `CompletionException`, both with the original exception
as the cause.

Exceptions that pass through dependent stages arrive wrapped as well. After a `thenApply`, an `exceptionally` handler
receives a `CompletionException` whose cause is the real error, and the `thenApply` body is skipped. Also, without an
executor argument the async methods run on `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, a poor place for blocking I/O. Fire-and-forget
futures need an explicit handler that logs, and production code should pass its own executor.
traps.interviewTip: Mention that fire-and-forget futures need whenComplete/exceptionally logging and a dedicated executor. Reviewers flag both in production code.

traps.title: wait() in an if instead of a while
options: Nothing: wait() only returns when there is a job for this thread
Deadlock, because wait() keeps holding the monitor
The second consumer to wake up can call remove() on an empty queue and get NoSuchElementException
IllegalMonitorStateException, because wait() is called inside synchronized
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Nothing: the consumer waits until it is notified, and a notification means a job is available.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates read wait/notify as 'sleep until the condition becomes true'. A notification only means 'something
changed, check again'. By the time a woken thread gets the monitor back, another thread may already have taken the
item. Threads can also wake up spuriously, with no notification at all.
traps.correct:
`notifyAll()` wakes both consumers, and they compete for the monitor. The first removes the only job. Then the second
gets the monitor, returns from `wait()`, skips the check (it was an `if`), and `queue.remove()` throws
`NoSuchElementException`. Spurious wakeups, which the Java spec explicitly allows, cause the same failure. The rule:
always call `wait()` inside a `while` loop that re-checks the condition.

Other facts interviewers probe: `wait()` releases the monitor while waiting, so there's no deadlock here. Calling
`wait()`/`notify()` without holding the object's monitor compiles but throws `IllegalMonitorStateException` at
runtime. And using `notify()` instead of `notifyAll()` can wake the 'wrong' kind of waiter and stall the system. In
real code, use a `BlockingQueue`, which already gets all of this right.
traps.interviewTip: Say 'wait always goes in a while loop' before they ask, then suggest BlockingQueue to show you would never hand-roll this in production.

traps.title: Executors.newFixedThreadPool has an unbounded queue
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Processing just gets slower; the pool has only 10 threads, so resource use is capped.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
The name 'fixed thread pool' suggests fixed resource use. The thread count is fixed, but the work queue behind it is an
unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue`. Nothing pushes back on the callers, so tasks pile up in memory faster than 10 threads
can drain them, and latency and heap usage grow until something breaks.
traps.correct:
`newFixedThreadPool(10)` uses a `LinkedBlockingQueue` with capacity `Integer.MAX_VALUE`. At 5 s per task, 10 threads
finish 2 tasks per second while 500 arrive, so the queue grows by about 498 tasks every second. Each task holds its
event in memory, so the heap climbs until GC pauses get long or an `OutOfMemoryError` hits. Queued events are lost if
the pod restarts, and callers never see an error that would tell them to slow down.

`newCachedThreadPool()` fails the other way: its maximum pool size is `Integer.MAX_VALUE` with a `SynchronousQueue`, so
it keeps creating threads until "unable to create native thread". Instead, configure a `ThreadPoolExecutor` explicitly
with a bounded queue, a rejection policy (`CallerRunsPolicy` slows the producer down), named threads, metrics on queue
depth, and timeouts on downstream calls. Shut pools down too: leftover non-daemon threads stop the JVM from exiting.
traps.fix:
```java
ExecutorService pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        10, 10, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000),                   // bounded backlog
        Thread.ofPlatform().name("webhook-", 0).factory(), // named threads (Java 21)
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());        // back-pressure instead of OOM

// Spring: ThreadPoolTaskExecutor with setQueueCapacity(...) and graceful shutdown.
// Java 19+: try (ExecutorService ex = ...) { ... } shuts down and waits on exit.
```
traps.interviewTip: Talk about back-pressure: a bounded queue plus a rejection policy turns a downstream outage into slower intake instead of an OOM in your own service.

traps.title: Virtual threads pinned by synchronized (Java 21)
options: Each virtual thread that blocks inside synchronized pins its carrier thread, so only about as many calls as CPU cores run at once
Virtual threads are slower than platform threads for I/O
synchronized isn't allowed on virtual threads, so the JVM falls back to a single thread
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Virtual threads just don't help with I/O-bound work, or the ConcurrentHashMap is the bottleneck.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Virtual threads are sold as 'write blocking code, get async scalability', so people assume every blocking call
unmounts the virtual thread. In Java 21 to 23, a virtual thread that blocks while holding a monitor (`synchronized`)
cannot unmount. It stays pinned to its carrier platform thread, and the scheduler has only about one carrier per core.
traps.correct:
Virtual threads run on a small ForkJoinPool of carrier threads (one per core by default). When a virtual thread blocks
on I/O or `sleep`, it normally unmounts and frees its carrier. In JDK 21 to 23, blocking inside a `synchronized` block
or method **pins** the carrier, so only about as many of these calls as you have cores make progress at once. In a
test with 2 carriers, 40 tasks each blocking for 100 ms took about 2,000 ms inside `synchronized` and about 100 ms
with `ReentrantLock`.

Fixes: use `ReentrantLock` around blocking sections on hot paths; upgrade to JDK 24+, where JEP 491 removed pinning for
`synchronized` (native frames still pin); and find pinning with the JFR event `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` (or
`-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads` on 21 to 23). Also, don't pool virtual threads, and limit access to scarce resources such
as DB connections with a `Semaphore` or the connection pool itself.
traps.interviewTip: Mention that JDK 24 (JEP 491) fixed synchronized pinning. Knowing the version history shows you actually follow the platform.

traps.title: @Transactional self-invocation (proxy bypass)
options: Spring fails at startup because of the self-call
Nothing: placeOrder() ran without a transaction, so the 3rd order stays saved with no payment
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Only the 3rd order is rolled back, because placeOrder() is @Transactional.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates think the annotation changes the method itself. In Spring's default proxy mode, a proxy object wrapped
around the bean starts the transaction, and only calls that go **through the proxy** are intercepted. Inside the same
class, `placeOrder(r)` is just `this.placeOrder(r)`, a plain Java call that never touches the proxy.
traps.correct:
Spring wraps `OrderService` in a proxy (a CGLIB subclass by default in Boot). The controller calls
`proxy.placeOrders()`, which has no annotation, so no transaction starts. The real object then calls
`this.placeOrder(r)` directly, and the transaction interceptor never runs. Each `orderRepository.save()` runs in the
repository's own short transaction (Spring Data repository methods are transactional) and commits immediately. When
`charge` throws there's nothing to roll back: orders 1 to 3 are all saved, and order 3 has no payment.

The same proxy rule means the annotation does nothing on `private` or `final` methods. Since Spring 6, class-based
proxies also intercept `protected` and package-private methods, but the call still has to come from outside the bean.
`@Async`, `@Cacheable`, `@Retryable` and `@PreAuthorize` all behave the same way.
traps.interviewTip: After explaining the proxy, point out the second smell: a remote payment call inside a DB transaction holds a connection and locks during network I/O. That's the senior-level observation.

traps.title: No rollback on checked exceptions by default
options: Yes, any exception thrown out of a @Transactional method rolls back
No, the transaction commits: by default only RuntimeException and Error trigger a rollback
Yes, but the audit row is kept
It depends on the database isolation level
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Yes: an exception escaping a @Transactional method always rolls back.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
'Exception means failure means rollback' feels obvious. Spring's default, inherited from EJB conventions, treats
checked exceptions as expected business outcomes that the caller can handle, so it **commits**. Many codebases use only
unchecked exceptions, so people never see this behaviour until a checked exception sneaks in.
traps.correct:
By default Spring rolls back only for `RuntimeException` and `Error`. A checked exception that propagates out of the
method still **commits** the transaction. Here the negative balance and the audit row are both written, and then the
caller gets the exception. Fixes: declare `rollbackFor = Exception.class` (or the specific type), make domain
exceptions extend `RuntimeException`, or, since Spring 6.2, change the global default with
`@EnableTransactionManagement(rollbackOn = RollbackOn.ALL_EXCEPTIONS)`.

An even more common variant: catching an exception inside the transactional method and only logging it. Spring never
sees the exception, so it commits whatever partial work was done. Either rethrow it, or mark the transaction explicitly
with `TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly()`.
traps.interviewTip: Mention the 'catch and log' variant as well. It's the version you actually find when reviewing legacy code.

traps.title: Caught exception, yet UnexpectedRollbackException
options: The order is saved; only the loyalty work is skipped
The order is rolled back and the caller gets UnexpectedRollbackException
Only the loyalty changes are rolled back; the order commits
The order is saved and the exception is logged twice
traps.commonWrongAnswer: The order is saved, because the exception was caught.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates picture `addPoints` as having its own transaction that fails on its own. With the default propagation,
`REQUIRED`, it **joins** the caller's transaction: one physical transaction, one fate. When the exception passes
through the inner proxy, Spring marks that shared transaction rollback-only, and catching the exception later can't
remove the mark.
traps.correct:
`addPoints` joins the existing transaction. Its proxy sees the RuntimeException, but as a mere participant it can't
roll back on its own, so it marks the whole transaction **rollback-only**. `placeOrder` catches the exception and
returns normally, so its proxy tries to commit. It finds the flag, rolls everything back (the order included) and
throws `UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction silently rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only`.

Options: give `addPoints` `propagation = REQUIRES_NEW` so it runs in its own physical transaction and its failure can't
affect the order; add `noRollbackFor` on `addPoints` if its failure is harmless; or, often best, run non-critical side
effects after the commit with `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)` or an outbox. The same trap appears
when you catch a repository exception, such as a constraint violation, inside a service transaction.
traps.interviewTip: Explain 'participating transaction, rollback-only flag' in one sentence, then offer the after-commit event as the design fix.

traps.title: REQUIRES_NEW: same-class calls and connection-pool deadlock
traps.commonWrongAnswer: (1) Yes, REQUIRES_NEW always commits separately. (2) Nothing special: it's still one request using the database.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates learn REQUIRES_NEW as 'an independent transaction' and stop there. They don't picture what it means
physically: the outer transaction is suspended but **keeps its connection and its row locks**, and the inner one needs a
second connection from the same pool. Under load, that doubles the connections each request needs.
traps.correct:
(1) Yes, as long as `record` lives in another bean. The inner transaction commits on its own before `charge` runs, so
the audit row survives the outer rollback. If `record` were in the same class, the self-call would bypass the proxy, no
new transaction would start, and the audit row would roll back with the payment.

(2) Each `pay()` holds one connection and then asks for a second. If 10 threads each hold one of the 10 connections
and all wait for another, none can continue. This pool deadlock ends only when Hikari's `connectionTimeout` (30 s by
default) throws `SQLTransientConnectionException`. A related trap: if the inner transaction touches rows the outer one
has already locked, it waits on a lock held by its own suspended caller until `innodb_lock_wait_timeout` expires.
Keep REQUIRES_NEW rare, size the pool for it, never use it in a loop, and consider writing audit data after completion
or through an outbox.
traps.interviewTip: Draw the connection math (N requests x 2 connections against a pool of N). Interviewers rarely hear candidates reason about pools.

traps.title: @Async self-invocation, void return and the default executor
options: Almost instant: the email goes to a background thread, and its exception is rethrown into signup()
About 3 seconds: the self-call bypasses the proxy, so the email is sent synchronously and its exception propagates into signup()
Almost instant, and the exception is silently lost
Startup fails: @Async methods must return a Future
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Almost instant, because @Async moves the email to a background thread.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
It's the same proxy misconception as with @Transactional: people believe the annotation changes the method. `@Async`
works only when the call goes through the Spring proxy, which hands the invocation to an executor. A call from another
method of the same bean is a direct Java call, so it runs on the caller's thread.
traps.correct:
`sendWelcomeEmail(u)` is really `this.sendWelcomeEmail(u)`. It skips the proxy and runs synchronously, so signup takes
about 3 s and a mail failure propagates straight into `signup()`. Move the method to a separate bean and it really does
run on an executor, which brings the next set of traps.

A `void` @Async method's exceptions never reach the caller. They go to the `AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler` (which logs
them by default), so return a `CompletableFuture` if you need the outcome. The async thread doesn't inherit the
caller's transaction, security context or MDC. And the executor matters: Spring Boot auto-configures a
`ThreadPoolTaskExecutor` with 8 core threads and an unbounded queue (or virtual threads when
`spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`). Plain Spring with no executor bean falls back to `SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor`,
which starts a new thread per task.
traps.interviewTip: Add that you'd send the email only after the signup transaction commits (an AFTER_COMMIT event or an outbox), so a rollback never emails a user who doesn't exist.

traps.title: Prototype bean injected into a singleton
options: 1,000, one per call, because it's a prototype
None until the first call, then one per request
traps.commonWrongAnswer: 1,000: prototype means a new instance every time it is used.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
'Prototype means a new instance each time' is true only for each time the container is **asked** for the bean.
Injection into a singleton happens exactly once, when the singleton is built. After that the singleton just holds an
ordinary Java reference, and Spring is never consulted again.
traps.correct:
Dependencies are resolved when a bean is created. `CheckoutService` is created once, so the container creates one
`PriceCalculator` for it, and every request reuses that instance. Here that also means `appliedRules` is shared by all
concurrent requests: rules from one customer's quote leak into another's, and many threads modify the list at once.

To get a fresh instance per use, ask the container each time: inject `ObjectProvider<PriceCalculator>` and call
`getObject()`, or use a `@Lookup` method. A scoped proxy (`proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS`) also works, but
it creates a new target on *every method call*, which surprises people. For one instance per HTTP request, use
`@RequestScope`. Simplest of all: make the calculator stateless and keep per-call state in local variables. Also note
that Spring doesn't call destroy callbacks on prototype beans.
traps.interviewTip: Say the cleanest fix is usually to make the bean stateless, and that you'd reach for ObjectProvider only when per-use state is really needed.

traps.title: Circular dependencies in Spring Boot 2.6+
options: It starts fine: Spring resolves cycles automatically with early references
It starts, but orderService is null inside InvoiceService
It starts, but one of the services is created twice
Startup fails: Boot rejects circular references by default (since 2.6) and reports the cycle
traps.commonWrongAnswer: It starts fine: Spring resolves circular dependencies through its three-level cache, as long as one side uses field injection.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Many tutorials, and older experience, describe Spring's early-reference cache that can resolve setter and field
cycles. That was the default until Spring Boot 2.5. Since Boot 2.6, circular references are **prohibited by default**.
Even when they're allowed, a cycle involving constructor injection resolves only if beans happen to be created in the
'lucky' order.
traps.correct:
Spring Boot 2.6+ sets `spring.main.allow-circular-references=false`, so the context fails to start with a report that
"the dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle" (a `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`
underneath).

Even with the property set to `true`, the result depends on creation order. If `OrderService` is created first, its
constructor needs `InvoiceService`, which in turn needs an `OrderService` that doesn't exist yet, so startup fails. If
`InvoiceService` is created first, its early reference can be handed over and startup succeeds. A design that only
starts in one bean order is fragile. A cycle is usually a design smell: two services that each know too much about the
other. Fix it by extracting the shared logic into a third bean or publishing an event instead of calling back. As a
last resort, inject one side with `@Lazy`, which gives a proxy resolved on first use.
traps.interviewTip: Treat the cycle as a design problem and refactor; mention @Lazy and allow-circular-references only as escape hatches.

traps.title: Field injection vs constructor injection
traps.commonWrongAnswer: It's just style: field injection is shorter, and Spring injects both the same way.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Field injection works, so the differences only show up later: in unit tests, in null-pointer bugs, and in classes that
quietly grow to a dozen dependencies. Candidates who haven't written many plain unit tests don't feel that pain. Many
also still believe a constructor needs `@Autowired`, or that constructor injection becomes unworkable with many
dependencies.
traps.correct:
Constructor injection is the recommended default, for concrete reasons:

- **Immutability**: fields can be `final`, so nobody ever sees a half-wired bean.
- **Fail fast**: a missing dependency stops startup instead of causing an NPE later, and the object can't exist
  without its dependencies.
- **Testability**: `new ReportService(fakeRepo, fakeRenderer, fakeMail)` works in a plain JUnit test, with no Spring
  context and no reflection-based `@InjectMocks`.
- **Design feedback**: an eight-parameter constructor makes a class that does too much impossible to miss.
- **Cycles** are detected at startup instead of being hidden.

Since Spring 4.3, a class with a single constructor needs no `@Autowired` at all. Field injection hides dependencies
and ties the class to a DI container. Setter injection still makes sense for genuinely optional dependencies, and field
injection is acceptable in test classes.
traps.interviewTip: Lead with testability and the 'too many constructor parameters' design signal. Those are the arguments seniors use, not 'the docs say so'.

traps.title: @Primary vs @Qualifier: which wins?
options: razorpayGateway, because @Qualifier narrows the candidates before @Primary is considered
traps.commonWrongAnswer: stripeGateway, because @Primary has the highest priority.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
`@Primary` is described as 'the default bean', and people read 'default' as 'overrides everything'. It's actually a
tie-breaker, used only when several candidates are still left. An explicit `@Qualifier` at the injection point is a
more specific request, so it filters the candidates first.
traps.correct:
Spring resolves by type first and finds both gateways. The `@Qualifier("razorpayGateway")` at the injection point then
filters the candidates down to the bean with that qualifier or name, so Razorpay is injected. `@Primary` matters only
when more than one candidate is left after qualifiers: an unqualified `PaymentGateway` parameter gets Stripe. With
neither annotation, Spring falls back to matching the parameter name against bean names, and if that fails it throws
`NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`. Relying on parameter names is fragile.

For a strategy pattern you don't need to pick a bean at all. Inject `List<PaymentGateway>` (all beans, ordered by
`@Order`) or `Map<String, PaymentGateway>` (keyed by bean name) and choose at runtime. Spring Boot also disables bean
definition overriding by default, so two beans with the same name fail at startup.
traps.interviewTip: Show the Map<String, Bean> strategy injection. It turns a resolution-rules question into a design answer.

traps.title: @Transactional(readOnly = true) misconceptions
options: No error, but the change is silently not saved
An exception: 'cannot write in a read-only transaction'
The change is saved; readOnly is only documentation
Startup fails: save() can't be called from a read-only method
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Either it throws an error, or readOnly is just a hint and the update goes through.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates treat readOnly as either a strict guard or a no-op. It's neither. It's an optimisation hint whose effect
depends on the stack. With Hibernate it turns off flushing and dirty checking, so entity changes simply never become
SQL: no error, no write, no log line.
traps.correct:
With JPA/Hibernate, Spring marks the session read-only and sets its flush mode to `MANUAL`. Hibernate keeps no
snapshots for dirty checking and never flushes, so `setActive(false)` produces no UPDATE. Calling `save()` doesn't
help: its own `@Transactional` joins the outer read-only transaction, and merging an already-managed entity changes
nothing. The method returns normally, and the change is lost.

Spring also marks the JDBC connection read-only, and some drivers enforce that. An explicit JPQL or native UPDATE
through MySQL Connector/J can fail with "Connection is read-only. Queries leading to data modification are not
allowed". Use `readOnly = true` on query methods: it saves memory (no snapshots) and CPU (no flush), and lets a routing
DataSource send queries to a replica. Never put it on a method that writes. A good, common pattern is read-only at
class level with writes overridden per method.
traps.interviewTip: Mention replica routing and Hibernate's skipped snapshots as the real benefits. That turns a gotcha into a performance answer.

traps.title: Open Session in View (spring.jpa.open-in-view)
traps.prompt:
At startup Spring Boot logs a warning: `spring.jpa.open-in-view is enabled by default...`. Lazy collections load fine
in your controllers, but the same code throws `LazyInitializationException` in a `@Scheduled` job.

Why the difference? Should you leave open-in-view switched on?
traps.commonWrongAnswer: OSIV keeps a transaction open for the whole request, which is convenient and harmless, so leave it on.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Because lazy loading 'just works' in controllers, people assume it's normal Hibernate behaviour, or that the
transaction lasts for the whole request. OSIV actually keeps the EntityManager (and, once it has one, a JDBC
connection) open for the whole HTTP request, **outside** any transaction. Scheduled jobs, message listeners and @Async
threads have no web request, so they get no such help.
traps.correct:
Boot registers `OpenEntityManagerInViewInterceptor` by default. It binds one EntityManager to the request thread, so
entities stay attached after the service transaction ends, and lazy associations load during controller code or JSON
serialization. Those loads run outside any transaction (auto-commit), one query per association: N+1 queries hidden
in your serializer. Once the request first touches the database, the connection is held until the response is
written, including during slow remote calls, so under load the pool runs dry. Dirty entities can also be flushed by a
later, unrelated transaction in the same request.

A `@Scheduled` job has no request, so its EntityManager closes together with the repository's transaction, and the
lazy access fails. Set `spring.jpa.open-in-view=false`, and load what each use case needs inside the service
transaction with fetch joins, `@EntityGraph` or DTO projections.
traps.fix:
```yaml
spring:
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false
```

```java
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public OrderDetailsDto getOrder(Long id) {
    Order o = orderRepository.findWithItemsById(id).orElseThrow();  // @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "items")
    return OrderDetailsDto.from(o);                                  // map while the session is still open
}
```
traps.interviewTip: Say you switch it off on new projects, and explain the connection-holding cost under load. That's the senior reason, not just 'it's an anti-pattern'.

traps.title: Are Spring singleton beans thread-safe?
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Yes: Spring manages the bean's lifecycle, so its beans are thread-safe.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Spring manages creation and wiring, so people assume it manages concurrency too. A singleton bean is one plain Java
object shared by every request thread, and Spring adds no locking. Code like this is fine in a single-threaded test
and fails only under concurrent load, which is exactly why it reaches production.
traps.correct:
Singleton scope means one instance per container, shared by all threads, and Spring does nothing to make it
thread-safe. Two kinds of shared mutable state break here under load. Many threads clear and fill `lines` at once, so
one customer's invoice can contain another's lines (or throw `ConcurrentModificationException`). And
`SimpleDateFormat` keeps internal mutable state, so concurrent `format`/`parse` calls produce wrong dates or
exceptions.

Stateless beans, holding only final references to other thread-safe beans and keeping per-call data in local
variables, are safe by design. That's why typical services and repositories are fine. Fixes: move per-call state into
local variables, use the immutable, thread-safe `DateTimeFormatter`, or use thread-safe structures when state really
must be shared. Changing the scope to prototype doesn't help if the bean is injected into a singleton.
traps.interviewTip: Answer 'singletons are shared, so they must be stateless or guard their state', and name SimpleDateFormat as the classic real-world offender.

traps.title: The N+1 select problem
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Add an index, or switch the associations to FetchType.EAGER.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
The code looks like one query, and in dev with five rows it's fast. Candidates don't see that every
`getCustomer().getName()` and `getItems().size()` on a lazy association silently fires its own SELECT. EAGER sounds
like the fix, but it changes *when* the extra queries run, not *how many* there are.
traps.correct:
This is the **N+1 select problem**. One query loads 50 orders, then each lazy access triggers another query: up to 50
customer SELECTs (fewer if orders share customers, since the persistence context caches each customer) plus 50 item
SELECTs. That's around 101 round trips instead of one or two.

Confirm it with SQL logging or statistics (`spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true`, or a datasource
proxy that counts queries), and assert query counts in a test. Fixes depend on the situation: `JOIN FETCH` or
`@EntityGraph` loads what this use case needs in one query; batch fetching (`hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50`)
turns N queries into a few `IN (...)` queries; a DTO projection selects exactly the columns you need, which is best for
read-only list endpoints. Switching to EAGER makes it worse, because every query that loads orders now pays for
customers, everywhere.
traps.interviewTip: Say how you'd *prove* it (a query-count assertion in a test, or Hibernate statistics). Measuring before fixing is what interviewers look for.

traps.title: LazyInitializationException and the wrong fixes
traps.commonWrongAnswer: LazyInitializationException; fix it with FetchType.EAGER or enable_lazy_load_no_trans.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates name the exception correctly, then reach for global switches that make it go away. Both suggestions hide
the symptom by changing loading behaviour for the whole application. Both also create performance problems that are
harder to find than the original exception.
traps.correct:
`findById` runs in the repository's own transaction. When it returns, the persistence context closes and `o` is
detached. `getItems()` returns an uninitialized proxy collection, and `size()` throws `LazyInitializationException:
failed to lazily initialize a collection ... could not initialize proxy - no Session`. In a web request the same code
may have 'worked' only because open-in-view kept the session open.

The right fix is to decide per use case what to load, inside a transaction: a `JOIN FETCH` or `@EntityGraph` query,
or mapping to a DTO inside a `@Transactional` service method. `EAGER` on a collection makes every load of Order fetch
its items, and no query can turn it off, which causes N+1 queries or huge joins elsewhere. `enable_lazy_load_no_trans`
opens a fresh session and connection for every lazy access: N+1 with extra connection churn and no transactional
consistency. `Hibernate.initialize(o.getItems())` inside a transaction also works, but it's clumsy.
traps.interviewTip: Reject both global switches by name and explain why. Interviewers use this question precisely to see whether you'll reach for EAGER.

traps.title: equals/hashCode on entities with generated ids
traps.commonWrongAnswer: 2: they are different tags with different names.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Using the id for equality feels natural, because the id *is* the row's identity in the database. But generated ids
don't exist until the entity is persisted. Until then every new entity has `id == null`, and
`Objects.equals(null, null)` is `true`, so all new entities look equal to each other.
traps.correct:
Both tags have a null id, so `equals` returns true and the hashes match. The set treats the second tag as a duplicate
and keeps only one, so a post saved with these tags would silently lose one. The opposite problem appears after
persisting: the id changes from null to, say, 7, so `hashCode` changes while the entity sits in a `HashSet`, and
`contains`/`remove` stop finding it (both effects verified in a plain Java simulation).

Lombok's `@Data`/`@EqualsAndHashCode` on entities is worse. It uses every field, including mutable ones and lazy
collections, which can trigger lazy loading, or a `StackOverflowError` with bidirectional relations. Safe options:
equality on a stable business key (a unique `sku` or `email`, ideally `@NaturalId`), or id-based `equals` that treats
a null id as 'not equal', combined with a constant `hashCode()`. Use `instanceof` rather than `getClass()` so
Hibernate proxies (which are subclasses) still compare equal.
traps.interviewTip: Explain both failure modes (null ids collapse before persist, hash changes after persist). Most candidates only know one of them.

traps.title: Dirty checking: no save() needed (and accidental writes)
options: No, you must call save() or nothing is written
Only if the entity class is annotated @DynamicUpdate
Yes, dirty checking flushes the change when the transaction commits
traps.commonWrongAnswer: No: without userRepository.save(u), nothing is persisted.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Spring Data's `save()` appears everywhere in tutorials, so it looks like the only way to write. Candidates think of
JPA like JDBC, where you change an object and then 'send' it. But entities loaded inside a transaction are *managed*:
Hibernate tracks them and writes changes for you. The flip side surprises people even more: changes you never meant
to persist get written too.
traps.correct:
Inside a transaction, `findById` returns a **managed** entity, and Hibernate keeps a snapshot of its loaded state. At
flush time (before commit, and before queries that might be affected) it compares each managed entity with its
snapshot and issues an UPDATE for every one that changed. So the rename is persisted without any `save()`. Calling
`save()` on a managed entity is redundant, because it merges the entity into itself.

The dangerous flip side: changing a managed entity just for display, such as masking an email before returning it,
gets **written to the database** at commit. Without `@Transactional`, `findById` runs in its own short transaction, the
entity is detached when it returns, and the change is silently lost. `@DynamicUpdate` only limits the UPDATE to the
modified columns, and `readOnly = true` switches dirty checking off.
traps.interviewTip: Bring up the accidental-write flip side (masking a field on a managed entity). It shows you've debugged this in real code.

traps.title: save() on a detached entity returns a different object
options: Yes: save() attached incoming, so the later change is flushed at commit
It throws 'detached entity passed to persist'
No: save() merged a copy; incoming is still detached, so the later change is lost
traps.commonWrongAnswer: Yes: after save() the object is managed, and the transaction flushes the later change.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
People assume `save()` always makes the object you pass in managed. That's true only for new entities, which go
through `persist`. For an entity that already has an id, Spring Data calls `merge`, which copies the state onto a
*different*, managed instance and returns that one. The argument stays detached, and later changes to it are ignored.
traps.correct:
`SimpleJpaRepository.save()` checks `isNew()`, which without a `@Version` field means 'the id is null'. Here the id is
42, so it calls `entityManager.merge(incoming)`. That loads (or finds) the managed Order 42, copies `incoming`'s state
onto it, and **returns the managed instance**. `incoming` itself stays detached, so setting CONFIRMED on it afterwards
is never flushed. Always continue with the return value: `order = repository.save(order)`.

Merging an entity built from JSON has another trap. Every field is copied, so fields the client didn't send (null in
the JSON) overwrite real column values with NULL. For updates, load the managed entity, apply only the allowed fields
from a DTO, and let dirty checking write the change. Related: with manually assigned ids, `isNew()` sees a non-null id
and `save()` merges as well, which costs an extra SELECT per insert.
traps.interviewTip: Mention that nulls from partial JSON overwrite columns on merge. That's the production bug behind this question.

traps.title: @ManyToOne is EAGER by default
options: 1, because customer stays lazy until accessed
2: one for orders and one for all customers
traps.commonWrongAnswer: 1: associations are lazy by default, so customers load only when accessed.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates learn 'JPA is lazy by default' from `@OneToMany`. But the JPA defaults depend on the association type:
to-one associations (`@ManyToOne`, `@OneToOne`) are EAGER and to-many are LAZY. And EAGER doesn't mean 'joined'. A
JPQL or Criteria query such as `findAll` loads an eager association with separate SELECTs.
traps.correct:
JPA defaults: `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` are `EAGER`; `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` are `LAZY`. `findAll()` runs a
query on Order only (`select o from Order o`), and Hibernate must then load the EAGER `customer` straight away.
Without batch fetching it issues one SELECT per distinct customer: 1 + 100 = 101 statements, even if your code never
reads `customer`. A single `findById` would use a join instead, which is why this often goes unnoticed in simple tests.

EAGER is a mapping-level decision that every query pays for and no query can switch off. Best practice: declare every
association `fetch = FetchType.LAZY` and fetch explicitly per use case with `JOIN FETCH` or `@EntityGraph`. Setting
`hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size` limits the damage to a few `IN (...)` queries.
traps.interviewTip: Recite the four defaults (to-one EAGER, to-many LAZY) and say you make every association LAZY from day one.

traps.title: orphanRemoval vs CascadeType.REMOVE
options: DELETE FROM order_item ..., because CascadeType.ALL includes REMOVE
An exception, because the item is now orphaned
Nothing: the row stays, and the item reappears when the order is reloaded
traps.commonWrongAnswer: A DELETE, because CascadeType.ALL includes REMOVE.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates read `CascadeType.REMOVE` as 'children get deleted when they leave the parent'. It actually means 'when the
parent is removed with `em.remove`, remove the children too'. Taking a child out of the collection is a different
operation, and on the inverse (`mappedBy`) side Hibernate doesn't even use the collection to write the foreign key.
traps.correct:
`CascadeType.REMOVE` (part of `ALL`) only cascades `entityManager.remove(order)`. Removing an element from the
collection isn't a remove operation. The collection is the inverse side (`mappedBy`), and the foreign key is owned by
`OrderItem.order`, which still points at the order, so Hibernate generates no SQL at all. The row stays, and on the
next load the item is back.

With `orphanRemoval = true`, Hibernate deletes any child removed from the collection, here with
`DELETE FROM order_item WHERE id = ?`. Use it only for children that can't exist without their parent (order lines,
not tags). Two related traps. Replacing the collection (`order.setItems(new ArrayList<>())`) when orphanRemoval is on
throws 'A collection with cascade="all-delete-orphan" was no longer referenced'; change the existing collection with
`clear()`/`addAll()` instead. And `CascadeType.REMOVE` on `@ManyToMany` deletes shared entities that other parents
still use.
traps.interviewTip: Contrast the two in one line: REMOVE follows the parent's deletion, orphanRemoval follows a child leaving the collection.

traps.title: Bidirectional mapping: only the owning side writes the FK
options: The item with order_id = NULL (or a NOT NULL constraint error)
The item, with order_id set correctly
No item row: cascade only works when both sides are set
Hibernate sets item.order automatically, so the row is correct
traps.commonWrongAnswer: The item row with the correct order_id, because the item is in the order's collection.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
In Java the relationship looks complete, since the order holds the item. But in a bidirectional mapping only the
**owning side** (the one with the `@JoinColumn`, here `OrderItem.order`) decides the foreign key. The `mappedBy`
collection is ignored when writing SQL, and Hibernate doesn't keep the two sides in sync for you.
traps.correct:
`cascade = ALL` makes Hibernate persist the item together with the order, so a row is inserted. But the `order_id`
value comes from `item.getOrder()`, which is null, so the row gets `order_id = NULL`, or fails with a constraint
violation if the column is NOT NULL. The collection side (`mappedBy = "order"`) is the inverse side: it's used for
reading, never for writing the foreign key. The object graph in the current persistence context is inconsistent too,
because `item.getOrder()` stays null until the data is reloaded.

The standard fix is helper methods on the parent that set both sides, and using only those. The same rule explains
why removing an item from the collection alone doesn't change the database.
traps.interviewTip: Use the terms 'owning side' and 'inverse side', and show the add/remove helpers. That's the complete answer.

traps.title: Pagination with JOIN FETCH happens in memory
traps.prompt:
This works in tests with 50 orders. Production has 2 million orders. What happens?

```java
@Query(value = "select o from Order o join fetch o.items",
       countQuery = "select count(o) from Order o")
Page<Order> findAllWithItems(Pageable pageable);   // called with PageRequest.of(0, 20)
```
traps.commonWrongAnswer: The database returns 20 orders with their items, using LIMIT 20.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates assume Hibernate always turns a `Pageable` into `LIMIT`. But a collection fetch join returns one row per
*item*, not per order, so limiting rows would cut an order's items in half. Hibernate refuses to do that in SQL.
Instead it paginates in memory, after loading everything, and only logs a warning.
traps.correct:
With `join fetch` on a collection, the SQL result has one row per order item. A `LIMIT 20` would return 20 *rows*,
which might be 3 orders with partial item lists. So Hibernate drops the LIMIT, fetches **all** matching rows, builds
every entity in memory, and then returns the requested page. It logs `firstResult/maxResults specified with collection
fetch; applying in memory` (HHH000104 in Hibernate 5, HHH90003004 in Hibernate 6). In production that means millions of
rows loaded per request: slow queries, huge memory use, OOM.

Set `hibernate.query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch=true` so this fails fast in tests. Fix it with two
queries: page over order ids with a normal LIMIT query, then fetch those orders with their items. Alternatively, page
plain orders and let batch fetching (`@BatchSize` or `default_batch_fetch_size`) load the items in one or two `IN`
queries. Fetch-joining a to-one association (`join fetch o.customer`) works fine with pagination.
traps.interviewTip: Mention the fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch flag. It shows you prevent this whole class of bug rather than fixing one instance.

traps.title: Lost updates and @Version
traps.commonWrongAnswer: @Transactional already prevents conflicting updates, and adding @Version locks the row so the second admin waits.
traps.whyPeopleGetItWrong:
Candidates treat a transaction as a lock on everything it reads. At READ COMMITTED, or MySQL's default REPEATABLE READ,
two transactions can both read the row and both update it, and the last commit simply wins. `@Version` is
misunderstood too: it doesn't lock anything. It only detects, at write time, that someone else changed the row first.
traps.correct:
Without a version column, both updates succeed and the last commit wins: a **lost update**, with no error anywhere.
